If i just started golf. Part 1

Thinking back, i think if i fixed my swing in this order, i would have saved myself alot of time. 

1. Grip - changing the grip later is such a pain, so just start with a neutral grip and if needed you can adjust slightly as you get better. Yes you can play good golf with a strong or weak grip, but better to start as neutral. 

2. Setup - im sure youve seen it too. The guy on the first tee with the odd setup. You know the swing is going to be just as odd, and it almost has to be. 

I think setup is important because It means less adjustments you have to do in the swing to get to a good impact position. 

3. Swaying - so hard to have a good consistent swing with ‘alot’ of swaying on the backswing. It just puts you in a position to do a whole lot of bad things. 

4. Early extension - think ive talked about this enough

summary: This TikTok by @itsjustcinema recommends the 1981 Hungarian animated film 'Son of the White Mare' (Fehérlófia), highlighting its unique and psychedelic visual style. It is intended for film enthusiasts looking for striking, cult-classic animation from the 1980s.
subtitle_text: Okay, okay. I promise this is not what it looks like. This is actually one of the greatest animated films you probably haven't seen. This is day three of sharing some of the weirdest, most obscure, and downright traumatic animated films from the 1980s. And today's film is easily one of the most visually striking films I have ever seen. This is Marcel Yankevich's the son of the White Mare. Three dragons rise from the underworld, destroy a kingdom, and drag its heroes into the darkness. But there is hope. Somewhere in the wilderness, a white mare gives birth to a boy with the strength of a god. When he learns what's happened to the kingdom, he sets off on a journey into the underworld to rescue his brothers and to pull a fallen kingdom back from the brink. I know, I know. That just sounds like a typical hero's journey, but I promise this film is unlike anything else you will ever see. The art style is just so bold and out there. Like, you really don't see animated films like this anymore. And one of my favorite choices is the lack of outlines in the illustrations. So Yankovic did this because he didn't want the characters to feel like they were sitting on top of the world. He wanted them to feel as if they're part of the environment. Yeah, the effect is deeply psychedelic, but I also feel like it reflects the emotional core of the story. Because in this world, nothing is isolated. There's no hard separation between the earth and the sky, between the hero and the mountains, between self and myth.

subtitle_text: Pretend you're a product manager at Uber and you have to answer the question of why cancellations have been up 10%, but rides have been down 15%. Are these just trips taken per day? Are they completed, or are they just requests that are being generated? Once you have those things clarified, you can also move into broadly questions about what's the time period on this? Is it sudden or has this been happening over a couple of months? Another question that you could ask is is there some sort of defect that's been happening on the app? That'll tell you if it's some and due to the internal engineering or something that is indeed problematic and that Uber needs to fix. Now, once you've asked all the clarifying questions, that's when it's time to move over to hypothesizing what problems could they be having that are driving cancellations up while also Reducing trips on a rider's end. This. This could mean things like seeing that the prices are too high whenever they're logging on to the app. They also might see that lift has a lower price than Uber does, and that's kind of dualling. So that's more external. Something else that could be just macro economic, is that the weather conditions that day aren't very stable. Now that you have your questions and your hypothesis, this for an interview, your interviewer would probably say something like, okay, let's go ahead and say that it had to do with prices being super, super high on the app. Now, how would you go about it? summary: Creator Evis Drenova discusses professional networking strategies and career growth within the technology industry. This video is a deep dive into building professional connections, likely saved by users looking to navigate the tech job market or improve their networking skills.
subtitle_text: Here are the three biggest mistakes that people make when they're trying to connect or network or talk to somebody that they don't know. And this is coming from somebody who gets a lot of emails, a lot of tik tok dms, a lot of linkedin requests from people who want to talk to me about, usually text stuff. Number one that they don't give a clear reason of what they want to talk about, why they want to talk about it, and why i'm the right person to talk to them about it. You're a lot better off sending a longer email or a longer DM, being really specific about what it is that you need and why that person is the right person to talk to you or hopefully to help you, then sending something vague like, hey, i'd like to spend thirty minutes to talk and get to know each other, or like, i'd love to learn more about your journey. Number two is asking for help on something or for, like, an introduction to somewhere or referral to something without making it clear that you've actually done the work to try and do it on your own or you've made progress towards that goal. I get a lot of emails or dms of people saying like, hey, I have an idea, can I talk to you about it? I'm like, everybody has an idea. Like, come back when you have something that you've built or You've gone out and you've tried to get customers or you've done something to show that you made some progress towards something. Like, you shouldn't be just reaching out to people to ask them for something if you haven't even tried to do it on your own. Like, that's no longer help. That's just you're trying to get the easy answer or you're trying to get an easy way to make some progress without putting in any of the work yourself. And number three, and i'm gonna go out on a limb and say everybody feels this way because we're all human and we all have egos. But if you get on a call with somebody, don't tell them that you're, like, the third networking call that you're doing that week. Like, we all wanna feel special. Like, don't tell me that i'm just another networking call, because that just makes me feel like you're using me. I know you're kind of just using me, and that's fine. That is the game that we play. But when you make it so, like, brazen and you make it so apparent, it really turns me off. I think it turns off a lot of people from wanting to help you. Like, if you're trying to get a referral or an intro to somebody and being like, oh, i've asked all these other people for intros as well, it's like, so why am I doing this for you? If all those other people Said no. Or if you have three referrals to YC and you're asking for a fourth one, it's just like, I don't wanna give you that referral because you've already gotten some. Like, what is my referral gonna do for you? Like, you've already gotten three more. Like, I know this sounds like, you know, we're being a little bit egotistical or like, maybe a little sensitive, but, like, we're all human beings at the end of the day, right? Like, you wanna make the people that you're talking to feel and ideally they should be like, they are specifically the ones who can help you and not just, you know, another introduction or another referral or another, like, whatever it is. Like, you should be targetedly reaching out to people, not just, like, reaching out to anybody who might be able to help you. I hope this helps. I think most people generally want to be helpful, but it is your job, if you're reaching out to somebody, to make it easy for them to help. And the way you do that is by giving them context and helping them understand specifically how they can help, and doing it in a way that's not so, like, i'm just using you for this thing. Like, you do wanna try and build an actual relationship, because ideally, it's not just a one time thing, and you could help each other in the future, and there's a way to go about that.

caption:
Homemade Chick-fil-a :)

Chick-fil-a sauce

½ cup mayonnaise 
3 Tbsp barbecue sauce
2 Tbsp honey
2 Tbsp yellow mustard
½ Tsp kosher salt 
½ black pepper
½ a lemon juiced

Chicken Brine

4 boneless skinless chicken thighs 
1 cups buttermilk
1 cup pickle juice
1 Tbsp paprika
1 ½ Tbsp garlic powder
1 tsp cayenne
1 tsp white pepper
1 tsp onion powder
1 Tbsp kosher salt

Dry Drede 

2 cups all purpose flour
½ cup potato starch
1 Tbsp paprika
1 Tbsp garlic powder
1 tsp onion powder
1 tsp MSG (optional)
1 Tbsp kosher salt
2 ½ tsp cayenne 
1 tsp ground black pepper

Waffle Fries

3 large russet potatoes
1 ½ Tbsp white vinegar
1 Tbsp salt
1.5 qt vegetable oil for frying

Pickles

1 small english cucumber or ½ a large one, sliced into thin rounds 
1 Tbsp pickling spice
1 cup white vinegar
1 cup water
2 Tbsp sugar
1 tsp MSG optional 
2 Tbsp kosher salt
2 sprigs dill

Assembly 

4 burger buns
4 slices pepper jack 
1 small head butter lettuce,
1 beefsteak tomato, thinly sliced
Lemonade (for the traditional experience) 

For the Chick-fil-a sauce, in a mixing bowl add, mayonnaise, barbecue sauce, honey, yellow mustard, kosher salt, black pepper and lemon. Mix until fully combined and set aside in the fridge. 

For the pickles, add your sliced cucumber to your mason jar along with the dill and pickling spice. In your sauce pot add white vinegar, water, sugar, MSG and kosher salt. Bring to a simmer then pour into the mason jar. Screw the lid on, let cool then refrigerate while you prep everything else. 

Prep the fries. Peel your potatoes and cut on a slice once on a wavy  mandoline, quarter turn, slice again and so on and so forth to get your waffle fries. If you don't have a wavy mandoline, you can cut the potatoes normally.

Add the potatoes to a large bowl and cover with ice water. Mix well to remove the starch, drain and set aside. 

Fill a large pot ⅔ the way with water, cover with a lid and bring to a boil. Once boiling add, white vinegar and salt.
 
Add your fries carefully to the pot and cook for about 2-3 minutes until slightly soft but not fully cooked. When you break one in half it should not snap like it's raw but it should be cooked with slight resistance. Make sure not to over cook this. Remove your potatoes to a couple of wire racks to cool. 

Heat your frying oil in a large pot to 330°F.

Carefully add your fries in batches and fry for 1-2 minutes until par cooked but not golden. Remove to a wire rack and set aside while we work on our chicken.

Chicken Brine: To a large bowl add, buttermilk, pickle juice, kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, cayenne and MSG. Add your chicken, mix well to coat and set aside in the fridge for 1 hour to overnight. Or use right away. 

In a large bowl add all purpose flour, potato starch, kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, cayenne and whisk to combine. Remove the chicken from the fridge. Coat the chicken in the dry dredge with no bald spots then dip back in the wet brine then back in the dry with no bald spots. Place your coated chicken on a wire rack and set aside.

Heat your oil to 350° F. Once your oil is up to temp, fry your chicken, 2 pieces at a time for about 6-8 minutes, until fully cooked and golden brown and crispy. Remove to a wire rack and repeat with all your chicken. 

Heat your oil to 375°F. 

Carefully add your par cooked fries to the oil in batches and fry for 1-2 minutes until beautiful golden brown and crispy. Remove to a wire rack and season generously with salt. 

Assembly, on a toasted bun add sauce, pickles, lettuce, tomato, chicken and cheese. melt however possible then add the sauced top bun. Serve with the fries and lemonade. Enjoy!
